blocks.prompt: The Loop You Have to Close
blocks.text: Nothing comes out of a battery until you close the loop. A battery is a can full of chemicals. The chemicals want to swap tiny bits called electrons. They cannot swap inside the can. The only road is out one end, through your flashlight, and back in the other end. That road is called a circuit. When you flick the switch, you finish the road. Electrons rush along it. The bulb glows. When you flick it back, the road breaks. The rushing stops. The bulb goes dark. The battery is still full. It is just waiting for you to close the loop again.

blocks.prompt: The Stack of Coins That Started It All
blocks.text:
In the 1780s an Italian doctor named Luigi Galvani was studying the legs of dead frogs. He kept noticing something odd. When a leg touched two different metals at once, a brass hook and an iron railing, the leg kicked. Galvani decided he had found a special electricity that lived inside animals.

His friend Alessandro Volta did not agree. Volta thought Galvani had the story backward. The two different metals were doing the work. The frog was only the wet part in between.

To prove it, Volta built a stack with no frog in it at all. He piled a disc of zinc, then a disc of copper, then a circle of cardboard soaked in salt water, and he repeated that pattern over and over. When he touched a wire to the top and the bottom, current flowed. Better than that, it kept flowing. Before this, people could only make a spark that jumped once and was gone. Volta had made electricity that ran like water from a tap.

He finished his stack in 1800 and called it a pile. We call it the first battery. The unit we use to measure electric push, the volt, is named after him.

(inference: a steady current can run a machine, a single spark cannot)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Three parts: anode, cathode, electrolyte
A AA battery pushes at 1.5 volts
The zinc inside is a gray powder
The electrolyte blocks electrons on purpose
A battery stores chemicals, not electricity

blocks.prompt: The Slow Fight Inside the Can
blocks.text:
Pop open a flashlight and the battery looks like a plain metal can. Inside, three parts are doing all the work.

The first part is the anode, the minus end. In a normal AA battery the anode is powdered zinc. Zinc atoms are willing to give up electrons, which are the tiny negative pieces of an atom. The second part is the cathode, the plus end, usually a black paste of manganese dioxide. It is hungry for electrons. The third part is the electrolyte, a wet chemical packed between them. The electrolyte is the strange one. It lets charged particles called ions drift through it, but it will not let electrons pass. That refusal is the whole trick.

The zinc has electrons to give. The cathode wants them. The shortest path is blocked by the electrolyte, so the electrons have to take the long way around: out of the minus end, through the wire, through the bulb, and back in at the plus end. On the way, they light the bulb. A battery does not store electricity. It stores chemicals that are eager to react, and it forces the reaction to pay a toll through your device on the way.

That explains the rest. A battery goes flat because the zinc gets used up, not because the electricity leaks out. Nothing happens until you close the switch, because until then the long way around is not a road at all. And a battery fades in the cold because chemical reactions run slower when they are chilled, so the pushing weakens.

(inference: it stores chemicals that are eager to react, and the electricity is made on the way out, not held inside)

blocks.prompt: The Rocking Chair in Your Pocket
blocks.text:
A regular battery is a one-way street. The chemicals react, the reaction finishes, and the battery is trash. For most of the twentieth century, that was simply the deal. Then chemists asked a stubborn question: what if the reaction could be run backward?

The answer sits in your phone. A lithium-ion battery does not burn its ingredients away. Instead it moves them. On one side is graphite, built of stacked carbon layers like a deck of cards. On the other is a metal oxide, usually containing cobalt or nickel. Lithium ions are small enough to slide into the gaps between those layers and park there. When the battery discharges, lithium ions leave the graphite, drift across the electrolyte, and slot into the metal oxide, while their electrons take the long way around through your screen. When you plug the phone in, the wall pushes them all back. Researchers nicknamed the design the rocking chair: the same lithium rocking from one side to the other and back, thousands of times.

Three chemists shared the 2019 Nobel Prize for this. Stanley Whittingham found in the 1970s that lithium could be tucked into a layered material. John Goodenough discovered that cobalt oxide made a far better home for it and pushed the voltage higher. Akira Yoshino swapped the dangerous lithium metal for graphite, which made the battery safe enough to sell. Sony shipped the first one in 1991. Every phone, laptop, and electric car since then stands on that work.

It is worth being honest about the cost. Cobalt is dug largely in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, sometimes by hand, sometimes by children. Lithium is drawn from brine under salt flats in Chile and Argentina, in landscapes where water is already scarce. A battery that runs a clean electric car is not clean where it comes from. Chemists now race to design cells with less cobalt, or none at all, and to recycle the metals in the batteries we have already built, which sit by the millions in drawers and landfills.

The rocking chair was a brilliant answer. What we dig up to build it, and what we do with it when it stops rocking, is a question we have not finished answering.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Energy density: watt-hours per kilogram
Gasoline beats lithium by about fifty to one
A battery must carry its own oxidizer
Density creeps up 5 to 8 percent a year
Pack prices fell nearly 90 percent since 2010
Grid batteries can be heavy, so cheap metals win

blocks.prompt: Why the Battery Is the Slowest Part of the Future
blocks.text:
Everything else in your phone got faster. The battery mostly did not, and understanding why explains a surprising amount about the century you are going to live in.

Start with the number that governs it all: energy density, the amount of energy packed into each kilogram. Gasoline stores roughly 12,000 watt-hours per kilogram. A very good lithium-ion cell stores about 250. Gasoline wins by nearly fifty to one. The gap narrows once you account for engines, which waste most of that energy as heat, while electric motors convert almost all of theirs into motion. But the gap does not close. That single ratio is why battery-powered airliners remain stuck on the drawing board while battery-powered cars are already on the freeway. A car can afford to be heavy. A plane cannot.

The reason the gap is so stubborn is that a battery must carry both halves of its reaction. Gasoline is only the fuel. Its other ingredient, oxygen, is free, and the engine scoops it out of the air on the way past. A battery brings its own oxidizer along, sealed inside the case, and pays for it in weight on every single trip. Worse, batteries obey chemistry, not manufacturing. Transistors got smaller because we learned to print finer lines, and a smaller transistor is a better transistor. But lithium will always weigh what lithium weighs, and the voltage between two materials is set by physics rather than by cleverness. Lithium-ion energy density has crept up around five to eight percent a year for three decades. It has roughly tripled since 1991. Computing power over the same period rose by a factor of millions.

Slow, however, is not nothing. Compounding at five percent for thirty years is what turned a battery that could run a camcorder into one that can move a two-ton car five hundred kilometers. The price fell even faster. A lithium-ion pack cost about 1,200 dollars per kilowatt-hour in 2010 and about 140 dollars by 2023, a fall of nearly ninety percent in a little over a decade. Falling price, not rising density, is what actually put electric cars in driveways.

The next problem is bigger than cars. Wind and solar are now among the cheapest electricity humans have ever generated, and both share the same flaw: they arrive when the weather says so, not when you flip a switch. A grid that runs on them needs somewhere to put an afternoon of extra sunshine until evening. That storage does not have to be light, which changes the whole calculation. A grid battery can be heavy, ugly, and built from cheap, common ingredients. Sodium, iron, and salt suddenly look attractive where cobalt does not. Engineers are also pouring effort into pumped water, spinning flywheels, and stacked concrete blocks, on the theory that the best grid battery may turn out not to be a battery at all.

Notice what has happened to the word. Volta's pile was a stack of coins that made a wire tingle. The thing we now call a battery is the hinge a clean electric century swings on, and the hinge is the slow part. Not because nobody is trying. Because it is made of atoms, and atoms negotiate harder than software does.
